notes: In 3.5, machine-configuration-compliance-status replaces machine-configuration-audit-mode to avoid a name giveaway. In 3.6, pipeline-cache-branch-isolation replaces pipeline-cache-artifact-purpose for the same reason. In 4.1, service-connection-project-sharing replaces service-connection-pipeline-authorization to avoid repeating variable-group authorization; triage-required-review-count replaces github-triage-push-permission to avoid repeating a permission-grant distractor.

cards.statement: The Bicep CLI translates Bicep files into Azure Resource Manager JSON templates during deployment.
cards.explanation: During deployment, the Bicep CLI produces an ARM JSON template. A team can choose Bicep authoring while keeping Azure Resource Manager deployment semantics.

cards.statement: Azure Resource Manager's what-if can resolve reference() values when comparing a template with live resources.
cards.explanation: What-if compares unresolved reference() expressions with current property values, so it can report a change even when deployment would preserve the value.
cards.misconception: What-if resolves runtime resource references into current values before calculating its comparison.
cards.volatilityNote: The expression-evaluation capabilities of ARM what-if can change.

cards.statement: Azure Resource Manager preserves omitted resource properties during an incremental redeployment.
cards.explanation: Incremental deployment reapplies a resource's properties. Include its non-default values because omitted properties can revert to defaults.
cards.misconception: Incremental deployment treats omitted resource properties as unchanged values.

cards.statement: Azure Resource Manager deploys an ARM template's resources in their listed order by default.
cards.explanation: Azure Resource Manager follows the dependency graph rather than file order. Independent resources deploy in parallel.
cards.misconception: The order of resource declarations determines the deployment order.

source.title: Define the order for deploying resources in ARM templates

cards.statement: Azure Resource Manager can record preflight validation failures in the activity log.
cards.explanation: Preflight validation errors appear in the activity log but have no entry in deployment history because deployment has yet to start.

cards.statement: The ARM template test toolkit's URI check can accept https://management.azure.com as a literal variable value.
cards.explanation: The toolkit flags hardcoded environment endpoints. Use the environment() function so a template adapts to the target Azure cloud.
cards.misconception: A valid Azure endpoint is accepted as a hardcoded value by the toolkit's URI check.

cards.statement: Azure Machine Configuration can apply operating system settings to Azure Arc-enabled servers.
cards.explanation: Azure Machine Configuration manages guest settings on Azure machines and hybrid machines connected through Azure Arc.

cards.statement: Azure Policy reports Azure Machine Configuration compliance from a VM's provisioningState value.
cards.explanation: Azure Policy reads complianceStatus from the guest assignment resource. A VM's successful provisioning state does not establish guest configuration compliance.
cards.misconception: VM provisioning success determines the guest configuration's compliance status.

cards.statement: Azure Machine Configuration reapplies settings in Apply and Monitor on in-scope VM tag edits with enforcement enabled.
cards.explanation: Enabled Azure Policy enforcement applies configuration when the machine resource changes. Updating an in-scope VM's Azure tag triggers that behavior.

cards.statement: Azure Machine Configuration uses policy metadata to create guest assignments for targeted machines.
cards.explanation: Definitions in the Guest Configuration category include guestConfiguration metadata. Azure Machine Configuration uses it to provision the machine's guest assignment.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines can reference a classic task group from a YAML pipeline during migration.
cards.explanation: Task groups belong to classic pipelines. Reuse equivalent steps through a YAML template when migrating to YAML.
cards.misconception: YAML pipelines consume existing classic task groups.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines exports a classic build designer's pipeline definition to YAML for migration.
cards.explanation: A pipeline created with the classic build designer supports YAML export. Classic release pipelines instead need their tasks exported individually.

source.title: Migrate your Classic pipeline to YAML

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines applies an organization-level run-retention policy across its projects.
cards.explanation: Azure Pipelines run-retention rules apply at project scope. Projects configure their own rules for pipeline runs.
cards.misconception: A central organization policy controls pipeline run retention across projects.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines retention leases extend a run's lifetime beyond the project's retention period.
cards.explanation: A retention lease preserves a selected Azure Pipelines run beyond normal cleanup, allowing production evidence to outlive ordinary development runs.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines preserves published pipeline artifacts when retention deletes their producing run.
cards.explanation: Deleting an Azure Pipelines run also removes its pipeline artifacts. Preserve the producing run when downstream consumers still need those files.
cards.misconception: Published pipeline artifacts survive deletion of their producing run.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines' duration report lists top tasks by duration for successful pipeline runs.
cards.explanation: The duration report shows task durations alongside the run-duration trend, helping engineers choose tasks to investigate for optimization.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines lets target-branch CI runs restore caches created under a pull request's merge-ref scope.
cards.explanation: Azure Pipelines places caches created by pull request validation in the merge-ref scope. Target-branch CI runs cannot read that scope, even when the cache key matches.
cards.misconception: Target-branch CI runs can read caches created in a pull request's intermediate merge branch.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines can queue jobs despite idle self-hosted agents when parallel-job capacity is exhausted.
cards.explanation: Registering self-hosted agents does not increase an organization's parallel-job capacity. Jobs need available capacity as well as an available agent.

source.title: Configure and pay for parallel jobs

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines' system detection marks a test flaky after it fails, then passes on a rerun within the run.
cards.explanation: With system detection enabled, Azure Pipelines uses a failed test's successful rerun within the same pipeline execution as evidence of flakiness.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines saves a new cache as soon as the Cache task finishes restoring dependencies.
cards.explanation: Azure Pipelines saves a new cache during Post-job: Cache after the job's steps succeed. Restoring a cache earlier in the job is a separate operation.
cards.misconception: The Cache task saves new cache contents during its restore step.

cards.statement: Azure automatically deletes a VM's system-assigned managed identity when an engineer deletes that VM.
cards.explanation: A system-assigned managed identity follows its Azure resource's lifecycle. Removing the VM also removes the identity's Microsoft Entra ID service principal.

source.title: What is managed identities for Azure resources?

cards.statement: Azure lets several self-hosted agent VMs use the same user-assigned managed identity.
cards.explanation: Assigning one user-assigned managed identity to several agent VMs gives those machines the same service identity for authorized Azure operations.

source.title: What is managed identities for Azure resources?

cards.statement: Azure DevOps evaluates a PAT's scopes independently of its owner's current permissions.
cards.explanation: A PAT's scopes restrict what it can do, while the owner's permissions remain its ceiling. Changing the owner's access changes the PAT's effective access.
cards.misconception: PAT scopes replace the permission checks for the user who owns the token.

cards.statement: Azure DevOps can change a user's access level through security-group permission settings.
cards.explanation: Azure DevOps access levels select available features; security groups grant or deny permission to use features and perform tasks.
cards.misconception: Security-group permissions select the user's access level and available feature set.

cards.statement: A Stakeholder can act on assigned release approvals in a private Azure DevOps project.
cards.explanation: Stakeholder access includes viewing releases and acting on approvals. An engineer can involve a business approver through that access level.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines uses project-level service connection roles to authorize edits after cross-project sharing.
cards.explanation: Once a service connection is shared, updates require an organization-level Administrator role in that connection's user permissions.
cards.misconception: Project-level service connection administration remains sufficient for editing a shared connection.

cards.statement: An organization owner can limit a GitHub App installation to selected private repositories.
cards.explanation: Selecting repositories narrows the installation's repository scope; the app uses its granted permissions within those repositories.

cards.statement: GitHub requires organization membership for a contractor to hold a repository's Admin role.
cards.explanation: GitHub can assign an outside collaborator any base repository role, including Admin, while keeping them outside the organization.
cards.misconception: A repository administrator must also be a member of its owning GitHub organization.

cards.statement: GitHub can count a Triage user's approval toward a repository's required approving reviews.
cards.explanation: GitHub lets Triage users submit reviews, but required approving reviews come from users with Write, Maintain or Admin access.
cards.misconception: Submitting an approving review makes it eligible to satisfy required reviews regardless of repository role.

cards.statement: Azure DevOps team administrators select the area paths that populate their team's backlog.
cards.explanation: Team administrators configure which project area paths appear on the team's backlogs and boards.

source.title: Define area paths and assign to a team

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines fetches linked Azure Key Vault secret values at runtime for the consuming pipeline run.
cards.explanation: A linked variable group holds selected secret names; a run retrieves their latest values from the vault.

source.title: Link a variable group to secrets in Azure Key Vault

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines uses a vault-wide secret selection for a variable group linked to Azure Key Vault.
cards.explanation: A linked variable group keeps an explicit selection of secret names. Adding a vault secret requires updating that selection before the group exposes it.
cards.misconception: Linking a vault makes its full secret inventory available through the variable group.

source.title: Link a variable group to secrets in Azure Key Vault

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines exposes secret variables as script environment variables by default.
cards.explanation: A script task needs an explicit env mapping to receive a secret variable as an environment variable.
cards.misconception: Secret variables receive the same implicit environment-variable mapping as ordinary variables.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines uses substring matches to mask fragments of secret variable values in task logs.
cards.explanation: Azure Pipelines applies secret masking to full-value matches rather than substrings; a field inside a structured secret can still appear in logs.
cards.misconception: Log masking redacts partial matches of a secret value.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines encrypts uploaded secure files on its server before pipeline tasks use them.
cards.explanation: The secure files library keeps the server copy encrypted at rest, including stored signing certificates and provisioning profiles.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines automatically deletes the Download secure file task's copy when a failed job finishes.
cards.explanation: The Download secure file task deletes its downloaded copy at job completion, including failed and canceled jobs.

cards.statement: GitHub Actions can sign in to Azure through a federated credential on a Microsoft Entra application.
cards.explanation: The federated credential tells Microsoft Entra ID which GitHub workflow identities it trusts for token exchange.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines can use system-assigned managed identities for workload identity federation service connections.
cards.explanation: The managed identity option for an Azure Resource Manager workload identity federation service connection uses an existing user-assigned managed identity.
cards.misconception: A federated service connection uses a system-assigned identity like the older agent-assigned authentication option.

source.title: Use an Azure Resource Manager service connection

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines withholds pipeline secrets from GitHub fork pull request builds by default.
cards.explanation: A fork pull request build needs an explicit opt-in to receive pipeline secrets, since a contributor controls its proposed build code.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines variable groups linked to Azure Key Vault map certificate objects into pipeline variables.
cards.explanation: The variable-group integration maps Azure Key Vault secret objects. It does not map the vault's cryptographic key or certificate objects.
cards.misconception: The variable-group link exposes certificate objects as well as secret objects.

source.title: Link a variable group to secrets in Azure Key Vault
